content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli is the edible flower head of Brassica oleracea var. italica, widely cultivated in temperate regions. When cooked, broccoli retains a bright green color, a mild flavor and a slightly crisp texture. It is used in side dishes, soups, salads and Asian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the same family as cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kale.
It is believed to have been domesticated in the Mediterranean over 2,000 years ago.
Raw broccoli contains more vitamin C than oranges, though some is lost during cooking.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for potential anticancer effects.
In Japan, broccoli is often served as “tenkatsu” – a battered and fried piece.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked broccoli provides a substantial portion of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Phytochemical compounds
items.content: Sulforaphane and other glucosinolates have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Broccoli is low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables, including broccoli.

items.title: Nutrient loss with cooking
items.content: Prolonged boiling can reduce vitamin C and some phytochemicals.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Broccoli may cause increased gas in some individuals due to its raffinose content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam broccoli for 5‑7 minutes until tender, add it to soups, stews, pasta, salads, or serve as a side dish with olive oil, lemon and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh broccoli in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container, where it stays crisp for up to 5 days. Store cooked broccoli in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like vegetables belonging to the cruciferous family. Fresh, cooked without added fat, they retain a crisp texture and a mildly nutty flavor. The vegetable is commonly used in side dishes, salads, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from Brussels, Belgium, where the vegetable was first cultivated on a large scale in the 16th century.
Each sprout is actually a miniature bud composed of many tightly packed leaves.
They are rich in glucoraphanin, a type of fiber that supports gut health.
There are over 300 varieties differing in size, leaf color, and taste.
When stored properly in the refrigerator, sprouts stay fresh for 2–3 weeks.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: One cup of cooked Brussels sprouts provides more than 100 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, which supports immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for cell division and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The sprouts contain quercetin and kaempferol, antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables can cause increased gas production in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: Large amounts of vitamin K may affect the efficacy of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Digestive difficulty for young children
items.content: Small sprouts can be hard for young children to digest; it is advisable to finely chop them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brussels sprouts can be eaten raw in salads, steamed, boiled, or sautéed without added fat (e.g., in a microwave). Steaming preserves most vitamins. A squeeze of lemon juice or a pinch of spices can enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sprouts in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container, where they stay fresh for up to 2 weeks. Do not wash before storing to avoid excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Instant coffee, not reconstituted (5233) is a dry powder made from roasted coffee beans with most of the moisture removed. The powder retains the aroma and flavor of regular coffee and is ready to consume without adding water.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Instant coffee was first produced commercially in the early 20th century.
Spray‑drying or freeze‑drying processes preserve most of the aromatic compounds.
In many countries instant coffee is popular in offices and for outdoor activities because of its convenience.
Some brands add stabilizers to improve solubility and taste.
Instant coffee can be plain or flavored with sugar, cream, or other additives.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Improves concentration
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Caffeine may boost metabolic rate and aid fat burning.

items.title: May reduce risk of certain diseases
items.content: Regular moderate coffee consumption is linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes and some neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: Convenient consumption
items.content: Instant coffee requires no special equipment, making it easy to include in the diet.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Certain instant coffees contain sugar, cream, or artificial flavors, which may be undesirable for specific diets.

items.title: Loss of some beneficial compounds
items.content: The drying process can reduce the amount of polyphenols and aromatic substances.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis sufferers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Place the instant coffee into a cup and pour hot water (80‑90 °C) over it. Add sugar, milk, cream, or plant‑based alternatives as desired. For a richer taste, use 1‑2 tsp per 200 ml of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a dry, cool place and seal it tightly after each use. Prevent moisture from entering to avoid clumping and loss of aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatless vegetable lasagna is a layered Italian dish that replaces traditional ground meat with a mix of fresh vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, eggplant, carrot) and tomato sauce, topped with mozzarella and parmesan cheese. The dish is rich in vitamins, fiber, and plant‑based protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetarian lasagna is often enriched with soy mince or tofu to boost protein content.
Traditional Italian lasagna dates back to medieval Italy, originally made with sheets of pasta, cheese, and sauce.
Adding vegetables makes the dish lighter and reduces calories compared with meat versions.
Gluten‑free versions use rice‑ or corn‑flour sheets instead of wheat pasta.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin A (as beta‑carotene) and folate, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Tofu or soy mince adds complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat and use of low‑fat cheeses reduces saturated fat, beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and red peppers contain lycopene and vitamin E, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and soy mince can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheeses and ready‑made tomato sauces are often high in salt; choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Calorie load from excess cheese
items.content: Using large amounts of mozzarella and parmesan raises calories and saturated fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Parboil the lasagna sheets, sauté the vegetables, combine them with tomato sauce and soy mince, layer with cheese, and bake for 25‑30 minutes at 180 °C until golden. Serve hot, garnished with fresh basil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked lasagna in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion, seal in freezer bags and freeze up to 2 months. Thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable belonging to the Amaranthaceae family. It is cultivated in temperate regions and is commonly used fresh in salads, sandwiches, as well as in cooked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is high in iron, but its absorption improves when paired with vitamin C.
Spinach was known in ancient Rome and Greece.
Its oxalate content can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.
There are several varieties: flat‑leaf, curly, and savoy (Latin).
Spinach is often used as a natural green food coloring.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate levels may increase the risk of kidney stones in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Raw leaves can carry pesticide residues; wash thoroughly or choose organic.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spinach can be added to sandwiches, salads, smoothies, or lightly sautéed or stewed. For sandwiches, use fresh young leaves, rinsed and patted dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store spinach in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container lined with a damp paper towel. Use within 3–5 days. Frozen spinach should be kept in an airtight bag for up to 6 months.
